shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of Czechia's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Ninety-four percent. {p} That's how rich the average Pole is, compared with the average Czech, this year: income per person, adjusted for prices. About sixty thousand dollars against sixty-four thousand. A gap of about four thousand. {pp} In 1995, Poland was at fifty-four percent of Czechia. Sixty percent by 1998. Seventy in 2011. Eighty in 2020. Ninety in 2024. {p} And the IMF's forecast ends in 2031 at ninety-six percent. Still not there. So the last few percent are the hard part. When does Poland actually pass?

In this series, Poland has been passing countries one after another. Japan this year. Spain next year, in the IMF's forecast. Italy, right after 2031. {p} Czechia is a different kind of race. It's a neighbor, both countries joined the European Union on the same day in 2004, and it's the richest of the four Visegrád countries: Poland, Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary. Poland passed Slovakia and Hungary by 2020. Czechia is the one it hasn't. {pp} <soft>Here's why it took so long, the year that changed this race, and the date the numbers point to.</soft>

Quick one before the chart: this is a series, and the next episode is Lithuania, a neighbor that was poorer than Poland in 1995 and is ahead of it now. Subscribe so you don't miss it. {p} Now, the race.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of Czechia's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: It started fast. {p} In 1995, the average Czech produced about fifteen thousand six hundred dollars a year, adjusted for prices. The average Pole, about eight thousand four hundred. By 2000, Poland had gone from fifty-four percent of Czechia to sixty-four. {pp} And then, almost nothing. For eight years, the line went sideways. In 2005 and 2006, Poland slipped back to sixty-one percent. In 2008, it was at sixty-four again, right back where it had been in 2000. {p} Czechia was running fast too: more than six percent a year in 2005 and 2006, with new car plants and foreign factories opening across the country. Then came 2009.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, Czechia (annual %); 2026 is an IMF estimate
shots.narration: Here's Czechia's economy, year by year, after inflation. {p} 2009: minus four point eight percent. Poland that year grew two point six, the only economy in the European Union that didn't shrink. In a single year, Poland jumped from sixty-four percent of Czechia to sixty-nine: the biggest one-year jump in the whole race. {pp} And that's the pattern. Since 1996, Czechia's economy has shrunk in five different years: 1997, 1998, 2009, 2012 and 2020. Poland's shrank in one: 2020, the pandemic.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH)
shots.title: Steady beat fast
shots.narration: Add it all up. Since 1995, Poland's economy has more than tripled in size, after inflation. Czechia's has almost doubled. Average growth since 2001: about three and a half percent a year for Poland, a little under two and a half for Czechia. {pp} And the last six years were the worst stretch for Czechia. Its economy in 2025 was only about five percent bigger than in 2019. Poland's grew about eighteen percent. In 2023, the Czech economy didn't grow at all, after inflation hit fifteen percent the year before. {p} Part of the reason: Czechia is built on cars, and on Germany. About a third of everything it sells abroad goes to Germany, and when German industry stalled, Czech factories stalled with it.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · general government gross debt (% of GDP), 2026 estimate and 2031 forecast
shots.title: Government debt, % of GDP, 2026
shots.narration: Now, what Czechia still does better. On jobs, it's a tie: unemployment is around three percent in both. But look at debt. Czech government debt this year: about forty-six percent of the economy. {pp} Poland's: about sixty-seven. And the IMF has that gap widening, to fifty-five against eighty-two by 2031.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ (NGDPDPC); Eurostat · regional GDP per inhabitant in PPS, % of EU average, 2024 (NUTS 2), via Czech Statistical Office
shots.title: Plain dollars, and the two capitals
shots.narration: Then, plain dollars. Without adjusting for prices, the average Czech produces about thirty-nine thousand six hundred dollars this year, and the average Pole about thirty-one thousand two hundred. In plain dollars, Poland is at seventy-nine percent, not ninety-four. {p} And then there's Prague. By the EU statistics office's numbers for 2024, the Prague region produces a hundred and ninety-two percent of the EU average per person, adjusted for prices. That's ahead of Brussels, Vienna and Berlin. Warsaw: a hundred and fifty-seven. {pp} Capitals flatter these numbers, because commuters are counted where they work, and the Prague region is just the city itself. Still, Warsaw is at about eighty-two percent of Prague: further behind than Poland is behind Czechia.
Now, the part that makes the last few percent so slow. {p} And if you're enjoying this, the subscribe button is right there. Lithuania is next.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · PPPPC gap in US$, real GDP growth forecasts (NGDP_RPCH), population (LP)
shots.title: The dollar gap
shots.narration: In dollars, adjusted for prices, the gap between the average Czech and the average Pole actually grew in the 2000s, and peaked in 2007 at about eleven thousand four hundred. This year, it's about four thousand. {p} But in the IMF's forecast, the closing slows right down. Poland grows about two and a half percent a year from 2027, Czechia about two. Half a point a year doesn't close a gap fast: by 2031, it's still about three thousand one hundred dollars. {pp} One thing does work in Poland's favor here, and it's not a happy one. Poland's population is shrinking, from about thirty-eight and a half million in 1995 to thirty-six million today, while Czechia's grew a little. Fewer people means more income per person, even from the same economy.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · PPPPC; parity years are Chartbound extrapolations of the 2016–2026 and IMF 2026–2031 paces, not IMF forecasts
shots.title: When does Poland pass Czechia?
shots.narration: So, when does Poland pass? {p} The IMF's forecast stops in 2031, at ninety-six percent. Beyond that, there's no official number, so here are two honest ones. {p} If the next few years look like the last ten, when Poland closed in on Czechia by about two percent a year, Poland passes around 2030. That's before the IMF's forecast even ends, so it would mean the IMF is being too cautious. {p} If the IMF's slower pace continues after 2031, it's around 2039. {pp} Nine years apart. The exact same spread we got for Germany, by the way: 2034 or 2043.

And there's a twist here too. Czechia's slowdown came from the same place as Germany's: expensive energy after 2022, and carmakers under pressure. Poland has something Czechia doesn't: a big home market of thirty-six million people. When exports collapsed in 2009, Poles kept spending, and that's a big part of why Poland never had a recession then. {p} In this race, being big and a little less exciting turned out to be an advantage.

<soft>So, your guess: 2030, 2039, or does Czechia hold on?</soft> Tell me in the comments. {p} If you're watching from Czechia: did the last few years feel as slow as the numbers say? {p} If you're in Poland: does it feel like you're about to pass Czechia? {p} And Lithuania: you're next, so tell me what I should know. I read every comment.
And if you missed it, Poland versus Germany is the big one: seventy-six percent, and two dates for catching up. That story is right here. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Poland Is 94% of Czechia. When Does It Pass?
yt.description:
Income per person, adjusted for prices (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): Poland was 54% of Czechia in 1995, 64% in 2000 — and still 64% in 2008. Then 2009 changed the race (Czechia −4.8%, Poland +2.6%): 70% in 2011, 80% in 2020, 90% in 2024, 94% this year, 96% in the IMF's 2031 forecast. Why Czechia stalled after 2019, where it still wins (debt, plain dollars, Prague vs Warsaw), why the last few percent are slow, and two dates for parity: ~2030 at the 2016–2026 pace, ~2039 at the IMF's pace.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP, LUR, GGXWDG_NGDP, PCPIPCH); Eurostat regional GDP per inhabitant in PPS, 2024 (via the Czech Statistical Office). Parity years are extrapolations, not IMF forecasts.
